title: How high does one more metre lift?
hook: Add 1 m to a rope round a ball, and 1 m to one round the Earth. Which lifts higher?

doesNotKnow: that adding a fixed length to the rope round any circle lifts it by the same height, 1 ÷ 2π of that length, however big the circle

misconception: An extra metre of rope round the Earth would lift it by a microscopic amount, far less than the same metre round a small ball.
objective: The learner can say that 1 m more rope lifts it about 15.9 cm round a ball and round the Earth alike, because the rope's length is 2π times the radius, so the extra metre adds 1 ÷ 2π to the radius whatever the size.

claims.text: The rope's length round a circle is 2π times the radius (circumference = 2πr).
claims.source: Definition of π as circumference ÷ diameter, with diameter = 2r; derivation.

claims.text: Adding length L to the rope raises the radius by L ÷ 2π, whatever the radius: for L = 1 m that is 1 ÷ 2π ≈ 0.159 m (15.9 cm), the same for a ball (r = 11 cm), a wheel (r = 35 cm) and the Earth (r = 6,378 km). For L = 2 m (the recall) it is about 0.318 m (about 32 cm).
claims.source: (2πr + L) ÷ 2π = r + L ÷ 2π. company/domains/briefs/checks/math-wave-j-check.mjs label G1 (0.1592 m for r = 0.11, 0.35 and 6,378,137 m; 1/2π = 0.159155). Stage: gapOf(r) = (2πr + 1) ÷ 2π − r in Demo.tsx, shown to 0.1 cm.

claims.text: The Earth's (equatorial) radius is about 6,378 km.
claims.source: WGS 84 semi-major axis a = 6,378,137 m (NGA TR8350.2). The gap does not depend on it.

recall.question: A rope hugs a giant round water tank all the way round. You add 2 m to it and lift it evenly. About how high is the gap?
recall.why: Each extra metre adds 1 ÷ 2π, about 16 cm, to the radius of any circle, so 2 m lift the rope about 32 cm, however big the tank.
